title: GMAT Focus Verbal Practice Test 20
instructions: Original exam-style practice test with answers and explanations.

questions.prompt: A pharmacy chain switched to dispensing generic medicines wherever permitted and reports that its medicine costs fell by 20 per cent. It concludes that generics are cheaper for the health system as a whole.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the conclusion?
options: A. Generic medicines are manufactured to the same standard as branded ones.
B. The chain negotiated discounts with generic suppliers.
C. Some prescribers specify branded medicines.
D. Generic prices vary between suppliers.

E. A significant number of patients switched to the generic version stopped taking the medicine after changes in appearance caused confusion, and their subsequent hospital admissions cost more than the savings.
questions.explanation: The claim is about the system, so a cost that appears elsewhere in that system is directly on point; the pharmacy's own budget improved regardless.

questions.prompt: A school district redrew its bus routes using scheduling software and reports that the average journey time for pupils fell by six minutes. Officials conclude that pupils now spend less time travelling.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, most seriously undermines the conclusion?
options: A. Some pupils walk to school.
B. The software cost less than expected.
C. The new routes drop pupils at collection points rather than at their homes, and the walk from those points is not counted in the journey time.
D. Journey times vary with traffic.
E. Drivers received training on the new routes.
questions.explanation: Part of the journey has been moved outside the measure, so the recorded fall need not correspond to less time spent travelling.

questions.prompt: A bank introduced automated alerts for unusual transactions and reports that confirmed fraud losses fell by a third. It concludes that the alerts prevent fraud.
questions.question: Which of the following would be most useful to determine in evaluating the conclusion?
options: A. How many alerts are sent each month
B. Whether the bank simultaneously tightened the rules for approving new accounts, through which much of its fraud had originated
C. Whether customers find the alerts intrusive
D. How the alerts are delivered
E. Whether other banks have similar systems
questions.explanation: A concurrent change addressing the main channel of loss would explain the fall without the alerts; this is the alternative that must be excluded first.

questions.prompt: A cycling shop notes that customers who buy stiff-soled shoes ride faster than customers who do not, and advertises the shoes as increasing speed.
questions.question: The advertisement is most vulnerable to the criticism that it
options: A. assumes that a difference between self-selecting groups of riders was produced by their equipment
B. does not specify the distance over which speed was measured
C. ignores the cost of the shoes
D. overlooks the importance of the bicycle itself
E. relies on customers' own reports of their speed
questions.explanation: Experienced and committed riders buy specialised shoes; the speed difference plausibly precedes the purchase.

questions.prompt: Every greenhouse on the Thornleigh nursery that is heated by biomass also has automated ventilation. No greenhouse with automated ventilation lost a crop to overheating last summer. Some greenhouses on the nursery lost a crop to overheating last summer.
questions.question: If the statements above are true, which of the following must be true?
options: A. Automated ventilation prevents overheating.
B. Most greenhouses are heated by biomass.
C. Biomass heating causes overheating.
D. Some greenhouses on the nursery are not heated by biomass.
E. Greenhouses without ventilation are older.
questions.explanation: Greenhouses that lost crops lack automated ventilation, and biomass heating implies that ventilation, so those greenhouses are heated some other way. B states a causal claim the premises do not establish.

questions.prompt: A company analysed its exit interviews and found that departing employees most often cite a lack of career progression. It concludes that improving progression would substantially reduce turnover.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the conclusion?
options: A. Exit interviews are conducted by the human resources department.
B. Some employees decline to attend an exit interview.
C. The company promotes from within where possible.
D. Turnover is higher than the industry average.
E. Departing employees avoid citing their manager or their pay in interviews conducted by their employer, and anonymous surveys of the same leavers give different reasons.
questions.explanation: The instrument systematically under-records the reasons that are awkward to say aloud, so the most-cited reason need not be the most important one.

questions.prompt: A city installed cameras that issue penalties to excessively loud vehicles and reports that measured night-time noise on the monitored streets has fallen. The council proposes installing them citywide to reduce noise everywhere.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, casts most doubt on the proposal?
options: A. The cameras are expensive to maintain.
B. Some residents did not notice a change.
C. The cameras operate only at night.
D. Noise on adjacent unmonitored streets rose by a similar amount, as drivers rerouted around the monitored sections.
E. Measurements are taken at street level.
questions.explanation: Displacement explains the local result; if drivers reroute rather than quieten, citywide installation faces a different problem than the trial suggested — though note it would also remove the alternative routes.

questions.prompt: A plant nursery began labelling which of its plants are attractive to pollinators and reports that sales of labelled plants rose while total sales were unchanged. It concludes that customers are choosing plants for their pollinator value.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, most strengthens the conclusion?
options: A. The labels are printed in green.
B. Sales of labelled plants rose most among varieties whose sales had previously been falling, and customer surveys record the label as the reason for purchase.
C. The nursery advertised the labelling scheme.
D. Labelled plants are priced the same as others.
E. Some customers buy plants for containers.
questions.explanation: It ties the shift to the label specifically, including for varieties that were losing ground for other reasons. D removes price as a confounder but adds no positive evidence.

questions.prompt: An employers' association argues that the training levy has failed, since the number of apprenticeships started has fallen since it was introduced.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, most weakens the association's argument?
options: A. The levy is paid by larger employers only.
B. Some employers find the levy administratively burdensome.
C. The levy replaced a system that counted short courses as apprenticeships, and the number of apprenticeships lasting more than a year has risen substantially.
D. Apprenticeship starts also fell in countries without such a levy.
E. The levy raises less revenue than forecast.
questions.explanation: A change in what the count includes means the falling number is not measuring the same thing; on the comparable measure the trend reverses.

questions.prompt: A council introduced hygiene ratings displayed in restaurant windows and reports that the average rating in the city has risen. It concludes that display has improved hygiene standards.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, most seriously undermines the conclusion?
options: A. Restaurants rated below three closed at a much higher rate than others after display began, and the average rose because the lowest-rated premises left the market.
B. Ratings are awarded on a five-point scale.
C. Inspections are unannounced.
D. Some restaurants dispute their ratings.
E. Customers report checking the ratings.
questions.explanation: Compositional change raises an average without any individual restaurant improving — though it is worth noting the exit itself may be an intended effect of the policy.

questions.prompt: A dairy cooperative argues that a rise in the farmgate milk price will increase the income of its member farms. A critic replies that a higher price will lead members to expand production, and that the resulting supply will push the price back down.
questions.question: The critic's reply would be most weakened if it were true that
options: A. milk prices are set annually
B. the cooperative sells into a market far larger than its members' output, so their expansion cannot appreciably affect the price
C. some members are near capacity
D. expansion requires investment in buildings
E. consumer demand for milk is stable
questions.explanation: If members are price takers in a much larger market, their own expansion cannot move the price, which is the mechanism the critic's reply depends on.

questions.passageText:
Popular events sell out within minutes and tickets then resell for multiples of their face value. The obvious inference is that promoters have misjudged demand. They have not: the underpricing is deliberate, and understanding why illuminates what a price is for.

Several motives operate together. A sold-out event is itself advertising, and a hall that fills at a lower price produces the crowd, the atmosphere and the coverage that a half-empty hall at a higher price does not. Performers with long careers have reason to avoid pricing out the audience that will buy the next tour, so a price that maximises this event's revenue may reduce lifetime revenue. And where an artist's reputation would be damaged by appearing to extract everything the market will bear, the low face value is a statement about the relationship rather than an error about demand.

The consequence is a gap between face value and market value, and that gap is a prize. Resellers capture it, and much of the industry's regulation is an attempt to decide who should. Restrictions on transfer, identity checks and capped resale platforms all reallocate the surplus, and each imposes costs: a ticket that cannot be transferred is worth less to a buyer whose plans may change.

The honest framing is that this is a distributional question wearing the clothes of a fairness argument. Someone will capture the difference between what the promoter charged and what buyers will pay — the promoter, the reseller, or the buyer lucky enough to be online at the right moment — and no arrangement makes the gap disappear while the underpricing that creates it remains deliberate.
questions.prompt: The passage indicates that the underpricing of tickets is
options: A. a miscalculation of demand by promoters
B. required by law in most jurisdictions
C. a consequence of resale platforms
D. deliberate, and explained by several motives operating together
E. confined to performers early in their careers
questions.explanation: The opening paragraph rejects the miscalculation reading explicitly.

options: A. production costs fall as attendance rises

questions.passageText:
Claims that a particular food raises or lowers the risk of a disease appear constantly and are frequently reversed. The pattern is not evidence that nutrition science is fraudulent; it is a consequence of the methods available for studying what people eat.

Randomised trials, the strongest design, are severely constrained here. A diet cannot be concealed from the person following it, adherence over years is poor, and the outcomes of interest take decades to appear, so trials tend to be short, small, and to measure a proxy such as cholesterol rather than the disease itself.

Observational studies therefore carry most of the weight, and they face two structural problems. Measurement is one: intake is usually established by asking people what they ate, and recall is unreliable in ways that correlate with the outcome, since people who are ill or overweight report differently. Confounding is the other and is worse. Someone who eats more vegetables also tends to smoke less, exercise more and have more money, and statistical adjustment can only correct for factors that were measured.

The field's better practitioners have responded by raising the bar. Findings are taken seriously when several methods with different weaknesses agree, when a dose-response relationship appears, and when a plausible mechanism exists. On that standard a small number of conclusions are secure and most single-study headlines are not. The distinction the public is rarely offered is between a field that knows a few things firmly and a literature that produces a great many weak results, which are not the same thing.
questions.prompt: According to the passage, randomised trials in nutrition are constrained because
options: A. participants cannot be recruited
B. diets cannot be concealed, adherence is poor, and outcomes take decades
C. such trials are prohibited by ethics committees
D. the results are always reversed
E. proxies such as cholesterol cannot be measured
questions.explanation: Those three constraints are given as the reason trials tend to be short, small and proxy-based.

questions.passageText:
Requiring a utility to serve every address at a uniform price is a policy with a clear rationale and an uncomfortable arithmetic. Delivering post, electricity or telecommunications to a remote household costs far more than delivering to a dense street, and a uniform tariff means the difference is paid by someone else.

The rationale is that these services are inputs to participation rather than ordinary goods. A household without a connection is excluded from services, employment and administration that assume one, and the cost of that exclusion falls on the excluded rather than on the market. Universal service obligations have been the standard remedy, financed either from the provider's profitable urban business or from a levy on all providers.

Two pressures have made the arrangement harder. Competition removes the cross-subsidy, because a new entrant serving only dense areas can undercut a provider carrying the obligation, and the obligation then becomes a competitive disadvantage rather than a shared cost. And technological change alters what counts as the service: an obligation defined around a copper telephone line does not deliver participation in a world organised around data.

The design question is consequently recurrent rather than settled. A defensible scheme must define the service in terms of what it enables rather than the technology that once delivered it, must finance it in a way that does not penalise the provider that carries it, and must be revised as the standard of participation moves — which is a demanding specification, and the reason most countries have rewritten these rules repeatedly.
questions.prompt: The rationale for universal service, as the passage presents it, is that the services are
options: A. natural monopolies
B. cheaper to provide at uniform prices
C. traditionally provided by the state
D. impossible to price accurately
E. inputs to participation rather than ordinary goods
questions.explanation: The cost of exclusion falls on the excluded rather than on the market, which is why the passage treats it as different from an ordinary good.

options: A. the technology currently in widest use
B. the cost of connecting the most remote household
C. what the service enables rather than the technology that once delivered it
D. the average household's consumption

questions.passageText:
Public libraries funded from taxation and open without charge are a nineteenth-century invention, and the arguments made for them at the time are not the ones usually offered now.

Their advocates were not, in the main, arguing for the pleasure of reading. The case was made in terms of an educated workforce, of sobriety — a reading room as an alternative to the public house — and of social stability, on the reasoning that a population with access to improving literature would be less inclined to disorder. Opponents objected to the cost, and to subsidising the leisure of others, in language that has survived remarkably intact.

The institution then outgrew its justification. Libraries became providers of newspapers, reference services for small businesses, warm public rooms, and, later, of internet access for households without it. None of these was in the founding argument, and the pattern is instructive: an institution created for one purpose acquired functions that the original purpose did not anticipate and would not obviously have supported.

This creates a difficulty when the case for funding must be made again. Measured against book lending alone, libraries look like a declining service. Measured against what they actually do — including functions that exist because no other institution provides a heated room where nothing must be bought — they are harder to assess and harder to defend, because the benefits fall on people whose alternative is nothing, and nothing is not a comparison that appears in any statistic.
questions.prompt: According to the passage, the original case for public libraries rested on
options: A. the pleasure of reading
B. an educated workforce, sobriety and social stability
C. the preservation of rare books
D. support for small businesses
E. the provision of warm public rooms
questions.explanation: The passage contrasts these founding arguments with the functions the institution later acquired.

And technological change alters what counts as the service: an obligation defined around a copper telephone line does not deliver participation in a world organised around data.

The design question is consequently recurrent rather than settled. A defensible scheme must define the service in terms of what it enables rather than the technology that once delivered it, must finance it in a way that does not penalise the provider that carries it, and must be revised as the standard of participation moves — which is a demanding specification, and the reason most countries have rewritten these rules repeatedly.

readingPassages.title: The Free Library
readingPassages.text:
Public libraries funded from taxation and open without charge are a nineteenth-century invention, and the arguments made for them at the time are not the ones usually offered now.

Their advocates were not, in the main, arguing for the pleasure of reading. The case was made in terms of an educated workforce, of sobriety — a reading room as an alternative to the public house — and of social stability, on the reasoning that a population with access to improving literature would be less inclined to disorder. Opponents objected to the cost, and to subsidising the leisure of others, in language that has survived remarkably intact.

The institution then outgrew its justification. Libraries became providers of newspapers, reference services for small businesses, warm public rooms, and, later, of internet access for households without it. None of these was in the founding argument, and the pattern is instructive: an institution created for one purpose acquired functions that the original purpose did not anticipate and would not obviously have supported.

This creates a difficulty when the case for funding must be made again. Measured against book lending alone, libraries look like a declining service. Measured against what they actually do — including functions that exist because no other institution provides a heated room where nothing must be bought — they are harder to assess and harder to defend, because the benefits fall on people whose alternative is nothing, and nothing is not a comparison that appears in any statistic.
